name: Turmeric
oneLineAnswer: Turmeric is a yellow spice. Its curcumin is studied for joint pain, but proof is not settled.
whatItDoes: Turmeric is the underground stem of a plant in the ginger family, grown in India and Southeast Asia.
Curcumin gives turmeric its yellow color, and it belongs to a group of compounds called curcuminoids.
Manufacturers often add piperine from black pepper so your body absorbs more curcumin.
Sellers promote oral turmeric for osteoarthritis, depression, allergies, itching, and high cholesterol.
For knee osteoarthritis, reviewers call early results positive but say better trials are needed.
whatWeDoNotKnow: NCCIH says we do not yet know whether turmeric or curcumin helps with any health purpose.
Curcumin studies are hard to compare, because products differ in curcumin content and in added plant ingredients.
Whether curcumin ointment applied to the skin eases knee osteoarthritis pain is unclear.
Early research suggests turmeric might change some fatty liver measures, but which ones is not clear.
Early research on mouth sores from cancer treatment looks encouraging, but it is not settled.
safetyNotes: NCCIH calls ordinary oral turmeric or curcumin likely safe for up to two or three months.
Oral turmeric can cause stomach upset, nausea, reflux, diarrhea, or constipation.
Products modified for better absorption have been tied to liver damage, and NCCIH warns they may harm your liver.
Turmeric supplements may be unsafe if you are pregnant.
Little is known about use above food amounts while breastfeeding.
In the United States, supplements are not approved by the FDA before they are sold.
Some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways, so NCCIH advises telling your provider what you take.
Turmeric supplement labels carry the line that the FDA has not evaluated their statements.

evidence.claim: Turmeric is a plant in the ginger family, grown commercially in Southeast Asia and India.
evidence.quote: Turmeric, a plant in the ginger family, is grown commercially in Southeast Asia and India.

evidence.claim: The part of the plant that is used is the rhizome, an underground stem.
evidence.quote: Its rhizome (underground stem) has been used for culinary and cosmetic purposes, among others.

evidence.claim: Curcumin, a major component of turmeric, gives the spice its yellow color.
evidence.quote: Curcumin, a major component of turmeric, gives the spice its yellow color.

evidence.claim: The health effects people claim for turmeric are attributed to curcuminoids, the group that includes curcumin.
evidence.quote: The health activities of turmeric are commonly attributed to curcuminoids, which include curcumin.

evidence.claim: Turmeric has a history of use in Chinese, Indian (Ayurvedic), Islamic, and Thai traditional medicine.
evidence.quote: Historically, turmeric has been used in Chinese, Indian (e.g., Ayurvedic), Islamic, and Thai traditional medicine systems

evidence.claim: Oral turmeric is promoted as a dietary supplement for osteoarthritis, depression, allergies, itching, and high cholesterol.
evidence.quote: Today, oral (taken by mouth) turmeric is promoted as a dietary supplement for a variety of conditions, including osteoarthritis

evidence.claim: NCCIH states that we do not know enough to conclude whether turmeric or curcumin is beneficial for any health purpose.
evidence.quote: We don’t know enough to definitively conclude if turmeric or curcumin is beneficial for any health purposes.

evidence.claim: Highly bioavailable curcumin formulations may harm the liver.
evidence.quote: Highly bioavailable formulations of curcumin, which enhance the body’s ability to absorb the curcumin, may harm your liver.

evidence.claim: Oral curcumin products vary in how much curcumin they contain and often include other plant substances.
evidence.quote: Oral curcumin products vary in how much curcumin they actually contain, and they often contain substances from other plants

evidence.claim: Combining curcumin with piperine, a substance from black pepper, is one way to improve bioavailability.
evidence.quote: Combining curcumin with piperine is one way to improve the bioavailability of curcumin.

evidence.claim: For osteoarthritis measures, NCCIH reports initial positive evidence and calls for higher-quality evidence.
evidence.quote: The initial evidence is positive; higher-quality evidence is needed to reach definitive conclusions

evidence.claim: It is unclear whether topical curcumin ointment affects pain from knee osteoarthritis.
evidence.quote: It’s unclear whether topical curcumin ointment has an effect on pain related to knee osteoarthritis.

evidence.claim: Initial research suggests oral turmeric or curcumin might improve some measures in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence.quote: Initial research suggests that oral turmeric or curcumin might improve some NAFLD measures

evidence.claim: Initial research suggests turmeric or curcumin might improve symptoms of oral mucositis from cancer treatment.
evidence.quote: Initial research suggests that turmeric or curcumin in an oral or mouthwash formulation might improve symptoms of oral mucositis

evidence.claim: Conventionally formulated oral turmeric or curcumin is likely safe in recommended amounts for up to 2 or 3 months.
evidence.quote: Conventionally formulated oral turmeric or curcumin (not modified to enhance bioavailability) is likely safe in the recommended amounts for up to 2 or 3 months.

evidence.claim: Oral turmeric can cause nausea, vomiting, acid reflux, stomach upset, diarrhea, or constipation.
evidence.quote: Oral turmeric can cause adverse effects such as nausea and vomiting, acid reflux, stomach upset, diarrhea, or constipation.

evidence.claim: Liver damage has been reported in some people who consumed bioavailable curcumin formulations.
evidence.quote: liver damage has been reported in some people who have consumed these bioavailable formulations

evidence.claim: The use of turmeric supplements during pregnancy may be unsafe.
evidence.quote: The use of turmeric supplements during pregnancy may be unsafe.

evidence.claim: Little is known about whether amounts above those commonly found in food are safe while breastfeeding.
evidence.quote: Little is known about whether it’s safe to use turmeric in amounts greater than those commonly found in food while breastfeeding.

evidence.claim: Dietary supplements are not approved by the FDA before they are sold to the public.
evidence.quote: Unlike drugs, dietary supplements are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) before they are sold to the public.

confidenceRationale: Identity, chemistry, and regulatory placement are supported by independent fetched sources (NCCIH plus openFDA labels, DailyMed, PubChem, and ClinicalTrials.gov). The usefulness and safety statements come mainly from NCCIH, a single synthesizing source, so confidence is not high.
gaps: MedlinePlus is not represented: its drug monographs are excluded by policy, and no MedlinePlus health topic or medical test page for turmeric was fetched.
PubChem has no compound record for turmeric itself; the name lookup returned HTTP 404 PUGREST.NotFound. Only curcumin (CID 969516) could be grounded in PubChem.
The DailyMed SPL detail endpoint returned HTTP 415, so only DailyMed's product list index could be read, not full label text.

The corpus classes turmeric as APPROVED_MEDICINE. No source fetched shows FDA approval of turmeric as a drug; openFDA labels show it as a dietary supplement ingredient or a homeopathic component of OTC products.
No fetched source covered interactions between turmeric and named prescription medicines; NCCIH gives only a general warning about herbs and medicines.
No fetched source stated safety beyond about two or three months of oral use, or long-term safety of bioavailable formulations.
No source fetched reported rates or numbers of liver injury cases; NCCIH and openFDA describe the signal without counts.
No individual dosing appears anywhere in this record, by design. The brief forbids reader-directed dosing, so label and trial amounts were left out.
Effectiveness claims could not be grounded in a second independent source; NCCIH was the only source that summarized trial evidence.
